docs.title: Data Visualization in R course Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the documentation for the data visualization course. This site is a live reference for R functions used in the course. Feel free to use this as a study reference, and contribute to it as well.

Data Transformation (dplyr)

Learn the core "verbs" for manipulating data frames. These functions allow you to reshape, filter, and calculate new data efficiently.

  • Data Transformation
    • Arrange | Group By | Mutate | Rename

String Manipulation

Essential tools for searching, replacing, and cleaning text data in R.

  • String Manipulation
    • Searching | Replacing | Cleaning

Visual Customization (ggplot2)

Take control of your plot's aesthetics. Learn to use built-in themes, fine-tune text and colors, and export your work.

  • Visual Customization
    • Themes | Theme Adjustments | Saving Plots (ggsave)

Conditional Graphics (Lattice)

A powerful system for creating multi-panel plots conditioned on variables, using a formula-based interface.

  • Conditional Graphics
    • Lattice Overview | Panel Customization

Advanced Visualization Concepts

Understand the different plotting paradigms in R and learn to create complex visualizations like heatmaps.

  • Plot Comparisons
    • Lattice vs. ggplot2 | Heatmaps

Updated with content from Lecture 11 (Themes), Lecture 12 (Lattice), and Advanced Concepts.

docs.title: Sorting Data
docs.text:
arrange()

Purpose

The arrange() function is used to reorder rows in a data frame based on the values of one or more columns. It is the equivalent of "sorting" in Excel.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The basic syntax is: arrange(data, column1, column2, ...)

docs.title: Basic Sorting
docs.text: By default, arrange() sorts in ascending order (smallest to largest / A to Z).

docs.title: How to use arrange()
docs.text: The basic syntax is: arrange(data, column1, column2, ...)

docs.title: 1. Simple Sorting (Ascending)
docs.text:
By default, arrange() sorts in ascending order (lowest to highest, or A-Z).

# Sort students by grade
students_sorted <- arrange(students, grade)

docs.title: 2. Descending Order
docs.text:
Use the desc() helper function to sort from highest to lowest.

# Sort students by grade (highest first)
students_desc <- arrange(students, desc(grade))

docs.title: 3. Multiple Columns
docs.text:
You can sort by multiple columns. If there is a tie in the first column, it uses the second column.

# Sort by major (A-Z), then by grade (highest first)
students_complex <- arrange(students, major, desc(grade))

docs.title: 4. Using with the Pipe Operation (%>%)
docs.text:
In modern R, arrange() is often used with the pipe operator to chain operations together.

# Filter students in IT major, then sort by grade (descending)
it_top_grades <- students %>%
  filter(major == "IT") %>%
  arrange(desc(grade))

docs.title: 5. Characteristics
docs.text:
• Missing values (NA) are always placed at the end, regardless of whether you use desc() or not.
  • It returns a new data frame; it does not modify the original one unless you assign it back.

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• rename: Used to change column names.
  • mutate: Used to create or transform columns.
  • group_by: Used to group data for operations.

docs.title: Saving Plots
docs.text:
ggsave()

Production Ready

The ggsave() function is the standard way to export your ggplot2 visualizations. It automatically detects the file type from the extension (e.g., .png, .pdf, .svg) and handles high-resolution output.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
ggsave(filename, plot = last_plot(), dpi = 300, width = NA, height = NA, units = c("in", "cm", "mm", "px"))

Argument Description filename The path and name of the file to save. plot The plot object to save (defaults to the last plot displayed). dpi Resolution (dots per inch). Use 300+ for print. width/height Physical dimensions of the output. bg Background color (e.g., "white", "black").

docs.title: Basic Save
docs.text:
library(ggplot2)

g <- ggplot(maacs, aes(x = logpm25, y = NocturnalSympt)) +
  geom_point()

# Saves the plot object 'g' to a high-res PNG
ggsave("my_plot.png", plot = g, dpi = 300)

docs.title: Advanced Export (Dimensions & Background)
docs.text:
From Lecture 11: 

# Saving with specific dimensions in millimeters and a black background
ggsave("outputs/maacs_plot.png", 
       plot = g, 
       dpi = 600, 
       width = 150, 
       height = 100, 
       units = "mm", 
       bg = "black")

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• Built-in Themes: Customizing the look before saving.
  • Theme Adjustments: Fine-grained control over colors.

docs.title: Grouping Data
docs.text:
group_by()

What does it do?

The group_by() function takes an existing data frame and converts it into a grouped data frame where operations are performed "by group." It doesn't change the data itself, but it changes how other functions (like summarize) interact with it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
group_by(data, column_to_group_by)

Power of Grouping

Grouping is most powerful when followed by summarize() to calculate statistics (mean, sum, count) for each group.

docs.title: Example: Grouping by Major
docs.text:
library(dplyr)

# Group students by their major
students_grouped <- group_by(students, major)

# When you print this, it will show "Groups: major" at the top
print(students_grouped)

docs.title: Why use group_by?
docs.text: group_by() is almost always followed by summarise() or mutate() to perform calculations within each category.

docs.title: Chaining with Summarise
docs.text:
# Calculate average grade per major
students_avg_by_major <- students %>%
  group_by(major) %>%
  summarise(avg_grade = mean(grade))

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• arrange: Used to reorder rows (can be used within groups).
  • mutate: Used to create or transform columns.
  • rename: Used to change column names.
  • string_manipulation: Search and replace text.

docs.title: Heatmaps: Visualizing Intensity
docs.text:
What is a Heatmap?

A heatmap uses colors to represent values in a matrix or a 2D grid. It is excellent for identifying clusters, hot spots, or correlations in large datasets.

docs.title: 1. Heatmaps in ggplot2
docs.text: In ggplot2, heatmaps are typically created using geom_tile() or geom_raster(). These functions require the data to be in "long" format (with columns for X, Y, and the Value).

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
library(ggplot2)

# Using a data frame with x, y, and z coordinates
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Old Faithful Density Heatmap")

docs.title: 2. Heatmaps in Lattice
docs.text: In Lattice, the levelplot() function is the standard tool for creating heatmaps. It can work directly with matrices or formulas.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
library(lattice)

# Using the built-in volcano dataset
levelplot(volcano, 
          col.regions = terrain.colors(100), 
          main = "Maunga Whau Volcano Topography",
          xlab = "Longitude", 
          ylab = "Latitude")

docs.title: 3. Key Differences
docs.text:
• ggplot2 (geom_tile): Better for categorical heatmaps (like a correlation matrix) and offers more control over the color scales and legends via the scale_fill_* family.
  • Lattice (levelplot): Highly optimized for 3D data and numeric matrices. It automatically includes a color key (legend) on the right.

docs.title: Tips for Better Heatmaps
docs.text:
1. Choose the Right Palette: Use diverging palettes (e.g., Red-Blue) for data with a meaningful center (like correlation) and sequential palettes (e.g., Blues) for magnitude.
  2. Order Matters: In categorical heatmaps, sorting your rows and columns (e.g., via clustering) can reveal patterns that are otherwise invisible.

docs.title: Conditional Graphics with Lattice
docs.text:
lattice package

The Lattice Philosophy

Lattice is designed for "Trellis" graphics—creating many small plots (panels) conditioned on one or more variables. It uses a formula-based interface (y ~ x | g) that is very powerful for scientific data.

docs.title: What are Trellis Graphics?
docs.text: Trellis graphics is a framework for data visualization designed to display multivariate data by partitioning it into multiple panels.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Conditioning: Partitioning a relationship (e.g., Weight ~ Height) into separate panels based on the values of another variable (e.g., | Gender).
  • Small Multiples: Instead of overcrowding a single plot, data is broken into a grid of clear, separate panels.
  • The "Strip": The label bar at the top of each panel that identifies the data subset.
  • Visual Consistency: Every panel uses the same axes and scales by default, allowing for immediate visual comparison across groups.

docs.title: Formula Interface
docs.text:
The core of every Lattice plot is the formula: response ~ predictor | conditional_variable

Component Meaning y ~ x Standard scatter plot. y ~ x \| g One panel for every level of variable g. groups = z Overlay different levels of z in the same panel.

docs.title: Core Functions
docs.text: Function Purpose xyplot() Scatter plots and line plots. bwplot() Box-and-whisker plots (and violin plots). stripplot() 1D scatter plots. dotplot() Cleveland dot plots.

docs.title: Example: Conditioned Scatter Plot
docs.text:
Using the airquality dataset:

library(lattice)

# One panel per month
xyplot(Ozone ~ Wind | Month, 
       data = airquality,
       layout = c(5, 1), # 5 columns, 1 row
       main = "Ozone vs Wind by Month")

docs.title: Example: Boxplots
docs.text:
# Boxplot of length by dose
bwplot(len ~ dose, data = ToothGrowth)

# Conditioned by supplement type
bwplot(len ~ dose | supp, data = ToothGrowth)

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• Lattice Panel Customization: How to add lines, medians, and custom logic to panels.
  • Scales and Layouts: Controlling the grid and axis limits.

docs.title: Lattice Panel Customization
docs.text:
panel functions

Low-Level Control

In Lattice, you don't "add layers" like in ggplot2. Instead, you provide a panel function that describes exactly what to draw inside every single panel of the grid.

docs.title: The Panel Function
docs.text: When you use the panel = argument, you are defining a small script that runs for every panel.

docs.title: Essential Panel Helpers
docs.text:
• panel.xyplot(x, y, ...): Draws the points.
  • panel.abline(h = ...): Draws horizontal/vertical lines.
  • panel.lmline(x, y): Draws a regression line.
  • panel.loess(x, y): Draws a smooth trend line.
  • panel.violin: Used with bwplot to create violin shapes.

docs.title: Adding a Median Line
docs.text:
library(lattice)

xyplot(y ~ x | f, 
  panel = function(x, y, ...) {
    panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)       # Draw the points first
    panel.abline(h = median(y),   # Add a horizontal median line
      lty = 2, col = "red")
  }
)

docs.title: Regression per Panel
docs.text:
xyplot(Ozone ~ Wind | Month, data = airquality,
  panel = function(x, y, ...) {
    panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)   # Points
    panel.lmline(x, y,        # Individual regression line per panel
      col = "blue", lwd = 2)
  }
)

docs.title: Creating Violin Plots
docs.text:
# Change the default panel from boxplot to violin
bwplot(len ~ dose, data = ToothGrowth,
       panel = panel.violin)

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text: • Lattice Overview: Basics of formulas and functions.

docs.title: Lattice vs. ggplot2
docs.text:
Choosing Your Tool

R has two primary systems for advanced data visualization: ggplot2 (based on the Grammar of Graphics) and Lattice (based on Trellis graphics). While both can create similar plots, their underlying logic is very different.

docs.title: Comparison at a Glance
docs.text: Feature ggplot2 Lattice Logic Layers (The Grammar of Graphics) Conditioning (Trellis Graphics) Syntax Iterative (+ operator) Single-call (Formula interface) Multi-panel Faceting (facet_wrap, facet_grid) Conditioning (y ~ x \| g) Customization Global theme() function par.settings and custom panel functions Output Type ggplot object trellis object

docs.title: ggplot2: The Layered Approach
docs.text:
In ggplot2, you start with a data frame and add layers one by one. This is very intuitive for building complex plots step-by-step.

ggplot(maacs, aes(x = logpm25, y = NocturnalSympt)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(~ bmicat)

docs.title: Lattice: The Formula Approach
docs.text:
In Lattice, you describe the entire plot relationship in a single formula. It is often faster for generating multi-panel "conditioned" plots.

xyplot(NocturnalSympt ~ logpm25 | bmicat, 
       data = maacs, 
       type = c("p", "smooth"))

docs.title: 2. Customization Philosophy
docs.text:
• ggplot2 uses a high-level theme() system. You can change everything from font sizes to background colors using named arguments.
  • Lattice provides low-level control through Panel Functions. If you want to add a custom line or calculation to every panel, you write a function that describes exactly what to draw inside the grid.

docs.title: 3. When to Use Which?
docs.text:
• Use ggplot2 if you want a modern, highly customizable "publication-ready" plot and prefer building layers iteratively.
  • Use Lattice if you are performing rapid exploratory data analysis, especially when you need to condition your plots on many variables simultaneously.

docs.title: Creating Columns
docs.text:
mutate()

Core Concept

The mutate() function is your primary tool for creating new columns based on existing ones or transforming existing columns. It keeps your original data intact while adding the results of your calculations.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: mutate(data, new_column = calculation_or_transformation)

docs.title: Example: Creating a Category
docs.text:
You can use mutate() with ifelse() to create categories based on values.

library(dplyr)

# Create a letter grade column based on numerical grades
students_mutated <- mutate(students, 
    grade_category = ifelse(grade >= 90, "A", 
                     ifelse(grade >= 80, "B", 
                     ifelse(grade >= 70, "C", "F")))
)

docs.title: Example: Mathematical Transformation
docs.text:
# Calculate age in months
students_age_months <- mutate(students, age_months = age * 12)

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• arrange: Used to reorder rows.
  • rename: Used to change column names.
  • group_by: Used to group data for operations.
  • string_manipulation: Search and replace text.

docs.title: Renaming Columns
docs.text:
rename()

Purpose

The rename() function is a specialized tool for changing column names. It is safer and more intuitive than base R methods because it follows a simple new_name = old_name pattern.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: The syntax is: rename(data, new_name = old_name)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
library(dplyr)

# Rename 'age' to 'student_age' and 'grade' to 'student_grade'
students_renamed <- rename(students, 
                           student_age = age, 
                           student_grade = grade)

docs.title: Key Rules
docs.text:
1. New Name First: You always put the new_name on the left and the old_name on the right.
  2. Selectivity: Only the columns you specify are renamed; all other columns remain the same.

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• arrange: Used to reorder rows.
  • mutate: Used to create or transform columns.
  • group_by: Used to group data for operations.
  • string_manipulation: Search and replace text.

docs.title: Cleaning Strings
docs.text:
trimws(), nchar(), and substr()

Final Polish

These functions are the "finishing touches" for text data, helping you trim whitespace, measure length, and extract parts of words.

docs.title: 1. trimws() (Trimming)
docs.text:
Removes leading and trailing whitespace.

text <- "   Data Visualization   "
trimws(text) # Result: "Data Visualization"

docs.title: 2. nchar() (Measuring)
docs.text:
Counts the number of characters in a string.

nchar("Baltimore") # Result: 9

docs.title: 3. substr() (Extracting)
docs.text:
Extracts a specific part of a string based on position.

# Extract the first 3 letters
substr("Baltimore", 1, 3) # Result: "Bal"

docs.title: String Manipulation Overview
docs.text:
String manipulation involves searching, editing, and cleaning text data. In R, while there are many packages for this (like stringr), base R provides powerful built-in functions that are essential for every data scientist to know.

Messy Data

Text data is often the messiest part of any dataset—containing unwanted spaces, inconsistent capitalization, or special characters. These tools help you fix those issues.

docs.title: Primary Guides
docs.text:
We have broken down string manipulation into three focused categories:

  • Searching: Find patterns using grep and grepl.
  • Replacing: Edit text using sub and gsub.
  • Cleaning & Measuring: Trim spaces and extract text with trimws and substr.

docs.title: Common Workflows
docs.text:
1. Cleaning: Removing leading/trailing whitespace with trimws().
  2. Subsetting: Extracting specific parts of a string with substr().
  3. Pattern Matching: Finding rows that contain a specific word with grepl().
  4. Replacement: Fixing typos or changing formats across thousands of rows with gsub().

Tip: When working with column names that have spaces or dots, string manipulation is often your first step in cleaning the data.

docs.title: Replacing Strings
docs.text:
sub() and gsub()

The Difference

  • sub() replaces only the first occurrence.
  • gsub() replaces every occurrence (Global sub).

docs.title: 1. sub() (Single Replacement)
docs.text:
Use this if you only need to change the first instance of a pattern in a string.

# Replace the first dot with a dash in column names
names(cameras) <- sub("\\.", "-", names(cameras))

docs.title: 2. gsub() (Global Replacement)
docs.text:
Use this for bulk cleaning where a pattern might appear multiple times.

# Replace ALL dots with dashes
names(cameras) <- gsub("\\.", "-", names(cameras))

Escaping Characters

Characters like . or + have special meanings. Use a double backslash \\. to treat them as literal text.

docs.title: Searching Strings
docs.text:
grep() and grepl()

Recall

Use these functions when you need to find rows or elements that match a specific text pattern.

docs.title: 1. grepl() (Logical Search)
docs.text:
Returns a logical vector (TRUE or FALSE). This is most commonly used for filtering data frames.

# Find all intersections that contain "Alameda"
has_alameda <- grepl("Alameda", cameras$intersection)

docs.title: 2. grep() (Index Search)
docs.text:
Returns the indices (positions) or the values of the matches.

# Get positions of matches
grep("Alameda", cameras$intersection)

# Get the actual names of the matches
grep("Alameda", cameras$intersection, value = TRUE)

Pro-Tip: Case Sensitivity

By default, these are case-sensitive. Use ignore.case = TRUE to find both "Alameda" and "alameda".

docs.title: Fine-Grained Theme Customization
docs.text:
theme()

The Ultimate Controller

While built-in themes provide a baseline, the theme() function allows you to modify every single non-data element of your plot, from legend position to the thickness of axis ticks.

docs.title: Core Elements
docs.text: The theme() function uses "element" functions to specify how to style different parts: - element_text(): Labels, titles, and text. - element_line(): Axis lines, gridlines. - element_rect(): Background boxes, legend boxes. - element_blank(): To remove an element entirely.

docs.title: Common Adjustments
docs.text: Parameter Purpose legend.position Moves legend ("top", "bottom", "none", etc.). plot.title Styles the main title. strip.text Styles the text in facet labels. axis.text Styles the numbers/labels on axes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Using the customization techniques from Lecture 11:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(maacs, aes(x = logpm25, y = NocturnalSympt)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ bmicat) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) + # Set global base size
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),          # Bold facet headers
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16), # Larger, bold title
    legend.position = "top"                             # Move legend to top
  )

docs.title: Data Transformation Overview
docs.text: Data transformation is the process of cleaning, reshaping, and preparing data for analysis. In R, this is primarily handled by the dplyr package, which provides a consistent "grammar" for data manipulation.

docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text:
To use these transformation functions, you need to install the dplyr package. Since dplyr is the core of data manipulation in R, many people install the entire tidyverse suite.

To use them in your script, you must load the library:

library(dplyr)
# OR
library(tidyverse)

Note

The base R functions mentioned in other sections do not require any installation. Only the dplyr functions listed below require this setup.

docs.title: The Core Verbs
docs.text:
Below are the primary tools you will use to transform your data:

  • Arrange: Reorder rows based on values.
  • Group By: Group data into subsets for analysis.
  • Mutate: Create or transform columns.
  • Rename: Change column names.

docs.title: Why Transform Data?
docs.text:
Rarely is raw data ready for visualization. You often need to: 1. Filter out irrelevant information. 2. Create new metrics (like calculating "Profit" from "Revenue" and "Cost"). 3. Sort data to highlight top-performing categories. 4. Aggregate data to see big-picture trends.

Reference: R for Data Science - Data Transformation

docs.title: ggplot2 Built-in Themes
docs.text:
Quick Style

Themes are the easiest way to change the entire "look and feel" of your plot with a single line of code. They handle background colors, gridlines, and default font sizes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: To apply a theme, simply add it to your ggplot object using the + operator.

docs.title: Standard Themes
docs.text: Theme Best For... theme_gray() Default. Good for data exploration. theme_bw() Printing and presentations (classic black & white). theme_minimal() Modern, clean look with no background. theme_classic() Traditional research paper style (no gridlines). theme_dark() High-contrast plots with bright colors. theme_void() Maps or diagrams where no axes are needed.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
library(ggplot2)

# Using the MAACS dataset from Lecture 11
ggplot(maacs, aes(x = logpm25, y = NocturnalSympt)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() # Applies the Black and White theme

docs.title: Comparison Example
docs.text:
# Minimalist approach
ggplot(maacs, aes(x = logpm25, y = NocturnalSympt)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()

# Completely empty (for custom annotations or maps)
ggplot(maacs, aes(x = logpm25, y = NocturnalSympt)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_void()

docs.title: Related Functions
docs.text:
• Theme Adjustments: Fine-grained control over text and colors.
  • ggsave: Saving your customized plots.
